intro: Out in Han district, in Eskişehir province, a face of rock has been carved into the front of a temple. This is the Midas Monument, also called Yazılıkaya: a Phrygian open-air sanctuary and rock-cut city of the 8th–6th century BC, famous above all for the 17 m-high Midas Monument itself. Let us begin.
history: The monument was carved into the rock in the 6th century BC for the Phrygian Mother Goddess, Matar, also known as Cybele. In 1800 it was rediscovered by William Martin Leake. But why 'Midas'? Its Phrygian inscription contains the word 'Midai', and that word gave the monument its name. The plateau around it is still called 'Midas City'.
structure-1: You are now standing before the Midas Monument, Yazılıkaya itself. This is the most famous of all Phrygian rock monuments, dedicated to the mother goddess Matar. Look up and let its carved face take shape before you.
structure-2: Here is the King's Altar, cut straight from the rock of Midas City. Ceremonies were held here; pause for a moment and imagine the rites that once unfolded on this stone.
structure-4: Now look at the great cisterns. Cut into the rock, these great basins stored the city's water, a reminder that this sacred place was also a living city.
structure-5: And here is the unfinished monument. Left incomplete, this monumental structure shows you what finished works hide: the ancient building techniques, caught halfway.
highlights: As you wander across the plateau, don't miss the rock-cut tombs.
facts: Did you know? The word 'Midas' in the inscription does not refer to the legendary king, but is an epithet of the Phrygian Mother Goddess Matar. Nor was the monument a tomb: it was an open-air temple for her statue. The rock monument rises seventeen metres high, and an old Phrygian inscription on it names Midas. It looks like a temple façade, yet there is no chamber behind it. Everything, even the door, is relief: the idea of a temple, drawn on rock.
outro: This brings our journey through the Midas Monument, Yazılıkaya to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
